cenas.sub: What it is and how to read the chart

cenas.texto: A signal marks the spot. You decide whether to enter.
cenas.fala: Hi, I'm Ricardo Garcia, and this is the Golden Zone Bootcamp from MoreThanMoney. It's two videos. In this first one we'll look at what the strategy is and how to read each element that appears on the chart. Before we start, one idea that runs through everything: the Golden Zone doesn't tell you to chase the price. When a signal appears, it marks a zone and waits for the price to come back to it. The final decision is yours, once you've validated the confirmations. We'll go slowly, one piece at a time.

itens: Video 1 · What the strategy is and how to read the chart
Video 2 · Confirmations, entry, plan and routine
cenas.fala: The bootcamp has two videos. In the first, you'll understand what the Golden Zone is, which market and which chart it was designed for, and what each element the scanner draws means: the yellow tick, the action zone, the exits, the invalidation and the gold flag. In the second video we get into the decision process: the four confirmations, the limit order, the stop, managing the trade, when not to enter, and a simple routine for your day. I suggest you watch the videos in order, and don't skip ahead to the entry part before you understand the chart.
Chapter one: so what exactly is the Golden Zone?

itens: Gold scalping, on the five-minute chart
The signal marks an action zone, not an entry
You decide, after four confirmations
Every new signal erases the previous one
cenas.fala: The Golden Zone is the MoreThanMoney scalping strategy for gold, on the XAUUSD symbol. It works on the five-minute chart, both for analysis and for entry. Scalping means the trades are short: you're looking for small moves, in the direction the market is already moving. It's not a strategy for catching the top or the bottom of the day. The core idea is something else. When a signal appears, the scanner doesn't tell you to buy or sell right away. It marks an action zone and waits for the price to come back to it. The difference in words is small, but in practice it's big. Someone who chases the price usually enters far from the place where the plan made sense. Someone who waits for the retest enters closer to the zone. Waiting also has a cost: some signals never return to the zone, and that is part of the strategy. The scanner shows the plan clearly. The decision still belongs to you.

itens: Asset: gold, on the XAUUSD pair
Timeframe: five minutes, for analysis and entry
Style: scalping in the direction of the trend
Watch it live, because every new signal erases the previous one
cenas.fala: The Golden Zone was designed for one asset, gold, on the XAUUSD pair. And for one working timeframe, the five-minute chart. That's where you see the signal, confirm the zone, validate the confirmations and decide on the entry. Notice a detail the guide stresses: every new signal erases the previous one. This means the Golden Zone is not a list of ideas kept on the chart. It's something you follow live, as it happens. If you only look at the chart once an hour, you'll miss signals, and you'll miss the reading of the moment the price reacts. So this is a strategy for someone who can be present, even if it's in short blocks of time. If you don't have that time, this may not be the right strategy for you. That's not a failure. It's a choice of style, and it's worth choosing well rather than forcing a strategy that doesn't fit your day.

cenas.titulo: Reading the chart, piece by piece
cenas.fala: Chapter two: how to read the chart, piece by piece.

This is what the chart looks like with everything on. At first glance it can look like a lot, and that's normal. In a few minutes you'll read each element in seconds. One important note before we continue: the charts you see in this bootcamp are illustrative. They're there to explain how the strategy works. They are not real results or market history, and they shouldn't be read as such. Now, what you can see. The fifty and two hundred exponential moving averages, which tell you the trend. The horizontal zones, which are levels where the price has already reacted in the past. The candles, coloured by direction. And the yellow tick, with the yellow box above it, which marks the action zone. The exit and invalidation lines don't appear yet. Why? Because there's no plan yet. We'll look at each element on its own.

cenas.titulo: Four pieces you need to recognise
itens: Yellow tick: a warning on the signal candle
Action zone: the yellow box where you wait for the price
Exit 1 and Exit 2: the targets, in green
Invalidation: the stop, in red. The gold flag marks the end
cenas.fala: Let's go piece by piece. First, the yellow tick. It appears over the signal candle, together with the yellow box, which is the action zone. The tick is a warning, not the entry candle. It only means the scanner found a setup that deserves attention. The parameters are still missing, and there's no trade yet. Second, the action zone. This is the area where, in theory, you place your limit order and wait for the price to return. Notice that the zone is a box, not a line, because the price rarely respects one exact value. Third, the exits. When the next five-minute candle closes, Exit 1 and Exit 2 appear, the two targets, in green. And the invalidation, in red, which is the level where the idea stops making sense. Without these three levels there's no trade. It isn't optional, it's the rule. Fourth, the gold flag. It appears when the price touches Exit 1, or the invalidation. When it appears, the trade is over: it paid, or it lost. With the flag in view, you don't enter. The flag is a closing piece of information. It tells you the moment has passed.

Now a sell signal. On a sell, everything flips. The action zone sits above the price, the invalidation sits even higher, and the exits sit below. The logic is the same, only the direction changes. What I want you to see is that the reading is symmetrical. Once you can read a buy, you can read a sell, as long as you remember to invert each piece. The averages also read the other way round. On a sell, the fifty average sits below the two hundred, and that's what gives you a downtrend. Here's one of the most common beginner mistakes: reading a sell as if it were a buy with the colours swapped. Swapping the colours isn't enough. You have to confirm that each piece is on the correct side. The structure of the reading is the same. Only the positions change.

cenas.sub: The sequence from tick to plan
cenas.fala: Chapter three: how you move from the tick to the plan, without skipping steps.

cenas.titulo: From the tick to the plan
itens: The tick appears over the signal candle
You wait for the next candle to close: only then is there a plan
Only then do the exits and invalidation appear
No complete plan, no trade
cenas.fala: The sequence is always the same, and the order matters. First, the yellow tick appears over the signal candle. At that moment you have nothing to execute yet. Second, you wait for the next five-minute candle to close. Only on that close do Exit 1, Exit 2 and the invalidation appear. Before that, what you have is a warning. Third, you read all the levels, and only then look at the confirmations. The temptation is to jump straight to the tick and start imagining the entry. The guide asks for a different order: first the reading, then the validation, and only then the plan. Once you get used to this sequence, you stop acting on impulse. If the next candle hasn't closed yet, there's no plan to read and no decision to make. This detail seems small, but it's what separates someone who waits from someone who gets ahead of the chart.

cenas.titulo: Five questions to ask the chart
itens: Is there a yellow tick, and has the next candle closed?
Is the yellow box over the signal candle?
Are Exit 1, Exit 2 and the invalidation drawn?
Is there a gold flag on the chart?
Are you looking at the current signal, not an old one?
cenas.fala: Before you look at the confirmations, five quick questions. Is there a yellow tick, and has the next candle closed? Is the yellow box over the signal candle? Are Exit 1, Exit 2 and the invalidation drawn? Is there a gold flag on the chart, meaning a trade that has already finished? And are you looking at the current signal, not one that the next signal has already erased? If the answer to any of these is no, stop there. There's no trade to analyse. Only when all five answers are right do you move on to validation.

itens: Entering on the tick, before there is a plan
Reading a sell as a buy with the colours swapped
Looking at a signal from hours ago, already erased
Drawing more lines than the chart needs
Giving weight to a trade that already has a gold flag
cenas.fala: Before we close this video, the most common reading mistakes. First, entering on the yellow tick without waiting for the plan. The tick is a warning, and a warning is not an order. Second, reading a sell as a buy with the colours swapped. We've already seen that's not enough. Third, looking at a signal from a few hours ago, which has already been erased by the next one, and treating it as if it were still alive. Fourth, drawing more lines than the chart needs. The Golden Zone already shows you the essentials, and extra lines only pull your attention away from the zone. And fifth, giving weight to a trade that already has a gold flag. Once the flag appears, the matter is closed. Write it in the journal and wait for the next signal.

itens: Keep the Golden Zone on one five-minute gold chart
Find ten yellow ticks in the history, without trading
For each one, note whether the plan appeared
Note how many ended with a gold flag
cenas.fala: Before the second video, a simple exercise. Pick a gold chart, on the XAUUSD pair, on five minutes, and keep the strategy running on that one only. Then, look back through the history for ten moments when a yellow tick appeared. For each one, note two things: whether the plan ever appeared, and whether the price came back to the action zone before reaching the exits or the gold flag. Don't trade. Only observe and note. This exercise trains your eye to see what the strategy actually shows, and in the second video you'll understand why this reading matters so much.

Entry inside the action zone

cenas.fala: Welcome to the second video of the Golden Zone Bootcamp. In the first we went through the chart, piece by piece. Now we move on to the decision. We'll look at the four confirmations, in the order you should validate them. Then how to place the limit order inside the action zone, where to put the stop, and how to read the two exits. We'll also look at when not to enter, which is just as important as entering. And at the end we'll close with a simple routine for following the strategy without spending the whole day in front of the screen. The scanner finds the signal and draws the plan. Everything that follows is your process, and that's what we'll build together.
Chapter one: the four confirmations, in order.

itens: Trend: the 50 average and the 200 average
Support and resistance: the zone has reacted before
Candle pattern: an engulfing candle in the direction
Imbalances: no unfilled price gaps near the invalidation
cenas.fala: Once you have the signal and the plan drawn, validate the four confirmations in this order. The more of them line up, the stronger the trade. The first is the trend. Use the 50 and 200 exponential moving averages on the five-minute chart. If the 50 is above the 200, the trend is up, and you only consider buys. If it's below, the trend is down, and you only consider sells. If the trend is against the signal, the guide is clear: let it go. The second is support and resistance. Ask yourself whether the action zone coincides with a place where the price has reacted in the past. If it does, mark that area on the chart. A zone that matches an old level gains strength. The third is the candle pattern. You're looking for a candle that confirms the direction. On a buy, a bullish engulfing, where the current candle engulfs the previous one. On a sell, a bearish engulfing. The fourth is imbalances. You confirm there are no unfilled price gaps near the invalidation. The guide sums this up in one line worth keeping: an efficient price path protects your stop.

Let's apply the four confirmations to a buy. The 50 average is above the 200, so the trend is up, and you only look for buys. The action zone coincides with an area where the price had already reacted before. That's the second confirmation, and it's marked in purple. Then the signal candle. It's a bullish engulfing, where the current candle engulfs the previous one, and it closes strongly. Third confirmation. Last, the path to the zone. There are no unfilled price gaps near the stop, so the price path is clean. Four out of four. That doesn't mean the trade will work. It means the readings agree, and the decision is now yours. With fewer confirmations, the decision is weaker, and the guide asks you to be more cautious. And if the trend is against you, you never get to this point at all.
Chapter two: the entry, the stop and the targets.

linhas: yellow box · limit order at the middle
cenas.fala: The plan has four levels, and each one has a job. The action zone is the yellow box, where you place the limit order. The guide suggests placing it in the middle of the zone, because that tends to give a better balance between risk and return. It's a suggestion, and you'll measure it in your journal. Exit 1 and Exit 2 are the targets, in green. If the price gets there, there's a profit. The invalidation is the stop, in red, and it's the level where the idea stops making sense. Don't put it tight against the signal candle. The guide asks for the stop to sit beyond the invalidation and beyond the most extreme wick of the previous candles, not just the signal candle. A wick that breaks the invalidation and takes you out of the trade is the classic mistake of a stop that's too tight. Before you send the order, calculate the position size. The scanner shows the levels, but you're the one who defines the risk.

itens: Wait for the next candle to close and read the levels
Validate the four confirmations
Place the limit order inside the zone
Stop beyond the most extreme wick
Calculate the size before sending
cenas.fala: Let's put this in sequence, at the guide's pace. One: wait for the five-minute candle after the tick to close and read the levels: action zone, Exit 1, Exit 2 and invalidation. Two: validate the four confirmations. If the trend is against the signal, let it go, and there's nothing more to do. Three: place a limit order inside the action zone. It isn't a market order. You want the price to come back to the zone and find you there. Four: the stop. Put it beyond the invalidation and beyond the most extreme wick of the previous candles. Five: confirm the targets, Exit 1 and Exit 2. And six, the most important, before you send the order: calculate the position size based on your account and the risk you decided on. A signal that looks good on the chart, but doesn't fit your risk, isn't a trade for you. Only after all of this does the order go to the market.

cenas.titulo: The order at the middle of the zone
cenas.rotulo: Order at the middle of the zone
cenas.fala: Here you can see the retest. The price came back to the action zone, the yellow box, and the limit order sits in the middle of it. The price touches the zone and turns back up, without reaching the invalidation. Notice that the stop sits beyond the lowest wick of the previous candles, not tight against the signal candle. That gives it room, without moving it away from the logic of the idea. The exits sit above, in green. This example shows an execution where the entry was at the planned place, the stop was at the planned place, and the management was the one written down beforehand. It isn't a promise that the move repeats. If this trade had gone to the stop, the execution would have been just as correct, and the loss would have been the one planned from the start.
Chapter three: when not to enter.

itens: On the yellow tick candle, still without a plan
Against the trend of the 50 and 200 averages
After the gold flag
Price already past Exit 2 without returning to the zone
Imbalances to fill near the stop
Stop tight only against the wick of the signal candle
cenas.fala: The guide has a clear list of when not to enter, and it's the part people forget most. First: on the yellow tick candle. There's still no plan, and a tick is not an order. Second: against the trend of the 50 and 200 averages. If the 50 is below the 200, you're not looking for buys, however nice the tick looks. Third: after the gold flag. The trade is over, and entering now means entering a different trade, with no plan. Fourth: when the price has already passed Exit 2 without returning to the zone. You're late, and in that case there's no entry. Fifth: imbalances to fill near the stop. If the price path is full of gaps, your protection is weaker. And sixth: a stop tight only against the wick of the signal candle. A stop like that is too tight, and the guide has already warned you what happens in those cases. If any of these situations is on the chart, you don't have a trade. You don't have to justify it to anyone. That's the process working.

cenas.kicker: When the zone doesn't come back
cenas.titulo: Went to Exit 2 without coming back: no entry
cenas.fala: Look at this example. There's a yellow tick and there's a zone. But the price rises beyond Exit 2 and never returns to the action zone. At no point was an entry possible, because the price never came back. The plan never appeared and the scanner removes the zone. The signal is over, with no entry, no gain and no loss. This is one of the most useful situations for a beginner, because it shows that not every signal has an entry. Some people find this frustrating, and that's understandable. But notice: if you had chased the price, you would have entered far from the zone, with a stop that no longer made sense. Not entering was consistent with the process, even if it didn't feel that way. Record in your journal that there was a signal and no trade.

cenas.titulo: Following without living on the screen
cenas.sub: A routine for the Golden Zone
cenas.fala: Chapter four: the following routine.

itens: Open the five-minute gold chart, live
Confirm the trend with the 50 and 200 averages
Look at the yellow ticks and the drawn zones
Validate the four confirmations before acting
Note in the journal, yes or no, and why
cenas.fala: The routine is simple. Before a session, you open the five-minute gold chart and follow it live, because every new signal erases the previous one. You confirm the trend with the 50 and 200 averages. You see whether there's a yellow tick and where the zones are drawn. When there's a signal, you validate the four confirmations, in order, without skipping any. If the answer is no, you let it go. And at the end, you note it in the journal, with a yes or no and the reason. This last step is the one most people skip, and it's the one that teaches you the most. You don't need to stare at the screen all day. You need to be present in the moments when the strategy can give a signal, and to follow the same process every time.

cenas.titulo: What to record for each signal
itens: Time, direction and whether there was a yellow tick
The four confirmations, yes or no
If you entered: where, the stop and the size
Result: Exit 1, Exit 2, stop or gold flag
Did you follow the process? What did you learn?
cenas.fala: The journal is the part that turns a strategy into learning. For each signal, record the time, the direction, and whether there was a yellow tick. Then the four confirmations, one by one, with yes or no. If you entered, record where the order in the zone went, the stop, and the position size. Then the result: did it reach Exit 1, Exit 2, the stop, or did the gold flag arrive before any entry? And finally, two questions worth answering honestly. Did you follow the process? And what did you learn from this signal? After a few weeks, the journal tells you where you're being consistent and where you're improvising. It doesn't give you magic answers. It gives you the pattern of your own behaviour, written by you.

We've reached the end of the Golden Zone Bootcamp. Remember what I said at the start: the strategy doesn't tell you to chase the price. It marks a zone and waits. You validate the confirmations, you calculate the risk, and you only enter when the process is complete. Do the exercises, practise first on a demo account, and write your journal from the very first signal, even if you don't enter. If you have questions, bring your cases to the community and to the live sessions at MoreThanMoney. I'm Ricardo Garcia. See you next time.
